title: AI games and copyrighting
author: devv11
selftext:
Obviously with the access to AI a lot of people are able to make games now which will probably produce a lot of plagiarisms.  
And I just stumbled upon this game (as for example) [PC Store Together](https://store.steampowered.com/app/4990940/PC_Store_Together/) which look like PC Builder Simulator ripoff. Sure he got a lof of new ideas and stuff but fundamentually it share the idea with PC Builder Simulator.   
Will it actually bother anyone? I mean at this point is almost impossible to create something completely unique that will not overlap with other games, cuz we got to a point when almost everything was created, inventing something new is a no.  
Does anyone even bother himself questioning if is ok to copy another game?

comments.author: Itchy_Ship2584

comments.author: benjaminabel
comments.body: What do you mean by “almost everything was created”? It only seems this way because a lot of ideas are getting copied a lot, but in no way “everything” was created. There are truly unique things appearing quite often.

replies.author: devv11
replies.body:
You can invent some good settings, story , etc but they will still somehow resembles things that were created in the past. Then gameplay, there is hundreds of thousands games were created since the creation of gaming, absolutely anything you will come up with - already existed in this or another form.  
So if I want to create a game I should always do inifity research whether some ideas were already copyrighted or not? In the end I will spent more time checking if is copyrighted instead of making the game

replies.author: Meatt
replies.body: I think this is a problem that you don't need to worry about. Just make something you want to make, and if you're not consciously copying something exactly or stealing code and art, then you're fine.

replies.author: CycleMother2006
replies.body:
Can you give an example of a modern game that is truly unique? Probably not. Because, for instance, going back to the days of Pac Man / Tennis for Two and you had the first implementations of movements controllers. Most games have some kind of movement controller that is directly derived from some game that came before it. Now days you just have drag and drop-in controllers depending on the engine, which already have a slew of basic functions. Simply by using Unreal you have a game with a slew of technology it's running that it didn't develop (lumen, nanite, the physics engine, etc). Any customized lighting/sky system you build on top of that is a derivation, not something unique.

Yes, some things are \*less\* of a copy because they diverge more from their parent, but they still have some foundation that is driving them.

In this particular comparison posed by OP, I'd say PC Store together has completely changed what it offers in that you're running a store. PC Build Simulator might overlap in the PC build part of it, but even comparing them is like saying Call of Duty is the same as Grand Theft Auto because they both have gunplay.

replies.author: benjaminabel
replies.body: That’s a very low-level comparison. You can as well say that every game has assets and therefore is not truly unique. I’m talking about store simulators, vampire survivors clones and other games that appear daily and you can’t even tell them apart. Truly unique are the ones you actually remember because they give you a unique experience. And there are not too many of them.

replies.author: CycleMother2006
replies.body:
I think you're conflating uniqueness with simply the origin of the genre. VSurvivors is not the best game in the genre, but it's certainly the most recognizable name and likely the bestselling (and not particularly close) because it happened to blaze the original path.

But if we shamed other games for trying to build on the formula, that'd be like shaming Eminem because he came after Vanilla Ice, or Genshin Impact for "copying" Breath of the Wild.

I don't disagree that there is a copyslop problem, but I think that's different from genuinely expanding on or riffing off an existing formula, which has been done across industries for most of human history. Sometimes the greatest innovations came from humans taking a thing (like bread) and saying, "What if I cut two slices and put some stuff inside?"

Another example is Stardew Valley. Arguably the closest thing you can get to a Harvest Moon clone. It just expanded on the existing formula verbatim, but is one of the greatest games in the genre today.

comments.author: caesium23
comments.body:
Plagiarism is using someone else's work and claiming it as your own. It's mainly applicable to media content (books, movies, music, graphics). A game that's similar to another game -- even a blatant knockoff -- usually isn't plagiarism, because they still had to do all the work to make a game. It's only really full-fledged plagiarism when it's not just a knockoff, but literally the original game files being reused without permission.

Just making a game that uses similar mechanics to another game, especially if you've added a lot of your own to it, is just called a genre.

replies.author: devv11
replies.body: So in this case then there will be no any lawsuits or troubles if I make a game that shares some similliar gameplay approaches etc?

replies.author: caesium23
replies.body:
Strictly speaking, plagiarism is not illegal, it's illegal to violate copyright, trademarks, or patents; those largely _overlap_ with what's likely to be considered plagiarism by most people, but plagiarism is subjective whereas those things have strict legal definitions. And I'm not a lawyer so I can't give you legal advice.

But that said, you're probably more likely to get hit by a car when crossing the street than you are to ever get sued as a result of making a game. Unless you're using assets without permission or copying literally an entire game beat for beat, this is almost certainly not something you need to worry about.

comments.author: Jack99Skellington
comments.body:
Ideas are not copyrightable. Mechanics can be patented, but rarely are, and when they are, the exact mechanics have to be copied (so you see why PalWorld got a pass).   
What does this mean for AI game development? Not much. But since we are talking copyright:  
Anything AI generated cannot be copyrighted in the US and Europe. <-- this is the most important.  
If you generate an image that says "MyCoolGame 5000", that image is not copyrightable. Anyone can use it. Same for that cool title song you generated. And that entire novel you generated, that goes along with your game. You can trademark things, but you can't copyright it.   
You may not like that. You may argue that your input to the prompt is enough to qualify your AI generated something for copyright. It is not. The courts have already ruled on this.

comments.author: TashLai
comments.body: Fundamentally, Stardew Valley shares the same idea with Harvest Moon. Going medieval copies from Rimworld. Rimworld copies from Dwarf Fortress. 3D shooters didn't fundamentally change since Wolfestein 3D. Every modern cRPG can be traced back to the 80th. As long as it's not carbon copy i'd say it's ok.

comments.author: DeanRayGames
comments.body: Copying popular games and trying to cash in on the progenitor's success is basically as old as video games themselves. When Atari had great success with pong, do you know how many pong clones there were? This is not a new problem. But what AI has done is make it ridiculously easy for people to rebuild sloppy clones of games quickly and saturate the market with them to a degree never before seen. It's a sad problem, and it's at a much higher level than ever before, but it's not a new one.

replies.author: devv11
replies.body: Sure but you always have a choice to not simply buy those games. I think steam won't let that opportunity of easy money slip away from them, so now we have AI slop festivals :D but again, that's what the world is now, AI will take over not only in gamedev but everywhere

replies.author: DeanRayGames
replies.body: Yeah, I agree. You always have a choice not to buy slop clones! And for a truly great game, any clone should stick out like a sore thumb. But it makes the homework a little "harder" for the gamer, because if you don't know which one is the original, and which ones are the clones, you have to do a little bit of work looking at each game, when they were published, etc. And in the past you had the problem of well-meaning parents buying a game for their kid that they thought was the one they wanted, but was really a sloppy clone. Haha. I don't think that happens much anymore, but wouldn't it be funny if a parent gifted their kid a slop clone game thinking they were getting them what they wanted?

comments.author: Practical_Remove_682
comments.body: i'm completely okay with this game. pc builder simulator never made multiplayer. so i'm glad this game is taking it on.

comments.author: mrpoopistan
comments.body:
Look to the fashion industry for how this is all going to play out: the brand is where the value now is.

As for "will it bother anyone?" the question is "Is there liability exposure here?" And that is a question for an IP law attorney, not a reddit thread. Bear in mind, the real question isn't whether it's legal; the real question is whether you can survival a legal attack long enough to get your attorney's fees paid back by the other party if you win. You can be on the right side of the law and still drown in litigation.

comments.author: Bed-After
comments.body:
The thing about copyright is that regardless of the laws on the books, it's only enforced with lawsuits. Toei, Disney, and Nintendo might be extremely letigious, but for 99.9% of companies in general, a lawsuit isn't worth the time and money. People getting away with blatant copyright infringement has been a thing since long before AI, and this has only accelerated the problem.

As far as AI games specifically, most of the people making rip-off games with AI aren't concerning themselves with the legalities. Worst case scenario for them isn't the people they ripped off suing. The worst case scenario is the original dev even finding out, deciding to alert Steam, and Steam taking the rip off game down and banning their account. That's a lot of steps where nothing might happen. Consequences are unlikely, and not very severe even if they do happen. t's not a big enough risk to make blatant plagarism not worth it.
